paragraphs.heading: Water dragged by the wind
paragraphs.text: Ekman transport is the movement of ocean surface water caused by the wind rubbing against it. It belongs to Ekman motion theory, which Vagn Walfrid Ekman first studied in 1902. Wind is the main source of energy for currents in the ocean, and Ekman transport is one part of the currents the wind drives. As the wind blows, its friction pulls the top 10–100m of the water along with it.

paragraphs.heading: Moving at an angle
paragraphs.text: The moving water does not simply follow the wind. The Coriolis effect pushes on it at a right angle to its motion, so it travels at an angle to the wind. In the Northern Hemisphere the water veers clockwise from the wind's direction, and in the Southern Hemisphere it veers anticlockwise. Fridtjof Nansen first noticed this on his Arctic expedition in the 1890s, when he saw sea ice drifting at an angle to the wind.

paragraphs.heading: Water that must be replaced
paragraphs.text: Ekman transport strongly shapes the chemistry and life of the oceans. The reason is a rule called hydraulic balance: water moved out of an area has to be replaced. Depending on the winds, this happens in one of two ways. Ekman suction draws water up, which is upwelling, and Ekman pumping pushes water down, which is downwelling.

paragraphs.heading: Three wind patterns
paragraphs.text: Three major wind patterns cause suction or pumping. The first is wind blowing parallel to a coast: if the surface water is pulled away from shore, suction follows, and if it is pushed toward shore, pumping follows. The second is the trade winds on both sides of the equator, which pull surface water toward the poles, northward on one side and southward on the other, so the water spreads apart and wells up at the equator. The third is large wind systems over the open ocean, which heap surface water into gyre-like mounds that gravity and mass balance then press downward.

paragraphs.heading: Suction feeds the sea
paragraphs.text: Ekman suction is the side of Ekman transport where water spreads apart and so wells up. The gap left behind pulls deep water up into the euphotic zone. That water is cold and full of nutrients, so it sets off phytoplankton blooms and starts a very productive ecosystem, and nearly half of the world's fish catch comes from upwelling areas. Examples lie along the Pacific coasts of California, Central America and Peru, and the Atlantic coast of Africa, where the currents head toward the equator. Suction also happens where the Polar Easterlies meet the Westerlies in subpolar regions, and where the Northeast and Southeast Trade Winds meet at the equator.

paragraphs.heading: Pumping starves it
paragraphs.text: Ekman pumping is the opposite side, where water piles together and sinks. Warm surface water that is poor in nutrients gets pushed down the water column, so the area becomes less productive. The sinking water also carries heat and dissolved oxygen into the deep. Off the Pacific coast of the Southern Hemisphere, northerly winds blow along the shore and the Coriolis effect turns the water 90° to their left, piling it against the coast. In the open ocean, pumping goes with gyres, as between 20°N and 50°N, where the trade winds give way to westerlies and surface water heaps up.
